title: Schooling in Potlatch and Palouse; meeting George
description: Wayne Comstock compares her unhappy years as a poor country student at Potlatch High School with her happy senior year at Palouse High School. She then explains meeting George at a basket social and their long courtship while he was away in the merchant marines.

title: Teaching school; George's eye injury; normal school
description: She recalls teaching the first four grades in her home school, including her little brothers, and her wages. A lead deposit poisoned George's eyes, delaying their wedding a year until Spokane surgery restored his sight. She attended Lewiston Normal School summers to earn her certificate.

title: Church membership; turning the farm over to sons
description: Wayne describes lifelong membership in Palouse's First Christian Church and raising their children there. Around 1953 they turned the farm over to their sons as they married, with George helping at hay and harvest.

title: Depression farm labor; thrashing years; coyotes and sow
description: During the Depression many relatives and helpers lived with them, and Wayne cooked for harvesting and threshing crews for ten hard years. She describes being alone with small children, chores and butter-making, a frightening encounter with an attacking sow, and George's early tractor and custom plowing.

title: Husband's outside work; women's work and income
description: A neighbor noted George worked year-round while others waited for spring. Wayne details the farm woman's work she did—milking, butter, gardening, setting hens, dressing chickens and selling fryers, and raising sheep—a wife's egg and butter money being her own.

title: Sheep and taxes; arthritis and Arizona winters; building the house
description: George paid his taxes with wool money. Wayne's arthritis in 1947 led the doctor to prescribe Arizona winters, and they traveled with trailers there for thirteen winters. In 1950 they built a new house on a corner of the forty, doing the painting and varnishing themselves, and later turned the original farm over to their son.

title: Building the new church; friends; golden anniversary
description: George was co-chairman of building Palouse's new church, working alongside their close friends. Wayne recalls the friend's husband's death in 1968 and her own golden wedding anniversary celebration with family and their former minister.

title: Caring for aging parents; mother's final years
description: Wayne's parents lived next door for 25 years; she helped with her father's asthma and later cared for her declining mother. After a hard winter of daily care, the family reluctantly placed her mother in a nursing home, where she lived three and a half years before dying at 91.

title: Retirement life; sister and family; grandchildren and adoption
description: Wayne describes contented golden years of gardening, ham radio, church fellowship and visiting the sick, and her sister's household next door. She talks about eleven grandchildren—three adopted—and babysitting, reflecting on the responsibilities and joys of grandparenting.

title: Children's illnesses; devoted country doctors; home births
description: She recounts chicken pox hitting all the children at once, a feared polio case, a baby's near-fatal infection treated in Spokane, a ruptured appendix, and scarlet fever. During the Depression two doctors made unpaid evening visits, which she repaid with dressed ducks. Finally she notes all her children were born at home.

title: Babies and childcare; helping new mothers
description: Wayne Comstock explains that a neighbor friend helped with her later babies, though she mostly nursed and cared for them herself. She recalls her three-year-old son Jerry's reaction to his new baby brother.

title: Jerry's premature birth; mother as midwife
description: Moving out of Princeton into a run-down house in September, she overworked herself cleaning it and her son arrived weeks early on December 7, weighing only five pounds. The doctor's car would not start on the icy morning, so her mother delivered the baby before he arrived, and the doctor scolded her for not calling sooner.

title: The family doctor; medical emergencies
description: She remembers the hot-tempered doctor who treated the whole family and her regret at never writing to thank him. He pulled her mother through gallstones, saved her brother after a mower nearly severed his leg, and saved her young son from a ruptured appendix, though the boy suffered incision pain for years.

title: Starting the nutrition club; Grange Hall
description: Once her three children were in school, she wanted a neighborhood club like those she had known in Princeton and arranged a home demonstration meeting at the Grange Hall. Only one woman, Ginny Morris, came, so she invited neighbors to her own home with university literature, and the club was born there forty years ago.

title: Anniversary parties; membership over the years
description: The club marked its thirtieth year with a celebration at the Grange Hall complete with flowers, refreshments, name tags, and a guest book, and members now plan a fortieth anniversary event. Of four charter members she is the only one left, and the club has shrunk from so many that two hostesses were needed to about a dozen.

title: Fundraising auctions; charitable giving
description: After tiring of fair booths, the club holds a November auction and potluck that raised over seventy dollars this year. The money goes to Care, a children's home, 4-H scholarships, and the youth ranch, and members rarely miss meetings.

title: Home economists; extension lessons
description: The club still gets monthly letters and occasional visits from home economist Jo Ann Anderson, whom they love. A notice in the Idahonian suggests she will be reassigned to clothing work across four counties, and the women fear losing their connection to her and to the University.

title: Gardening programs; district and state conventions
description: She attended a well-run university gardening day for the clubs last March. The clubs also sponsor district conventions each spring and occasional state conventions in Moscow, with younger members like her daughter-in-law representing the club at council meetings.

title: Senior Citizens Club in Palouse
description: Asked what she and her husband George enjoy in their later years, she describes their Senior Citizens Club in Palouse. It meets monthly for a potluck dinner followed by a talk, slides, or a film borrowed from a library.
